claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn has an FCC initial lattice.
The modeled initial state has minimized pre-existing dislocation density and a controlled distribution of vacancy clusters.
Loading is applied at strain rates of 10^8–10^10 s^-1 and temperatures of 100–600 K along <11-1> and <110> orientations.
Shockley partial dislocations nucleate through cooperative activation at pre-existing vacancy clusters.
Local lattice distortion around vacancy clusters lowers the energy barrier for partial-dislocation nucleation.
Shockley partial dislocations generate intrinsic stacking faults that propagate on {111} planes.
Dislocation nucleation initiates exclusively at vacancy clusters.
The maximum yield stress is significantly higher for <11-1>-oriented samples than for <110>-oriented samples.
The yield stress is predicted to be 15–20% higher for <11-1> than for <110>.
The <11-1> loading orientation maximizes resolved shear stress on the {111}<112> slip system relative to <110>.
The larger resolved shear stress in the <11-1> orientation causes earlier dislocation nucleation and a higher macroscopic yield stress.
The HCP-like regions are transient stacking faults stabilized by high defect density rather than a thermodynamic HCP phase.
The HCP-like regions lack long-range HCP order.
Stacking-fault formation will produce broadening and shifting of FCC diffraction peaks without distinct HCP reflections.
A continuous, reversible change in the FCC (111) peak and I(111)/I(200) ratio during heating, without new stable-HCP reflections, would discriminate stacking faults from a phase transformation.
An otherwise standard FeNiCrMn baseline without vacancy clusters has lower yield strength.
In the baseline without vacancy clusters, dislocations nucleate at grain boundaries or surface defects.
The mechanism applies only when vacancy clusters dominate nucleation, as in single crystals or highly textured samples without significant grain-boundary effects.
Above the melting point, amorphization dominates the material response.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says that maximizing resolved shear stress causes earlier dislocation nucleation while also producing a higher yield stress. Because the proposed yield event is tied to nucleation, earlier nucleation and higher nucleation-controlled yield stress are not coherently reconciled.

The initial state is described as a single-crystal-compatible state with controlled vacancy clusters, whereas the baseline invokes grain-boundary nucleation and random orientation. This changes both defect population and microstructure, so it is not a clean vacancy-cluster control.
